title: “Monks, how does a monk live as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island,…
content: “Monks, how does a monk live as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, seeking no other refuge? Monks, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body internally, ardent, diligent, mindful, clearly comprehending, to remove covetousness and sorrow in the world; abides contemplating feelings as feelings … mind as mind … phenomena as phenomena, ardent, diligent, mindful, clearly comprehending, to remove covetousness and sorrow in the world. Thus, monks, a monk lives as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, seeking no other refuge.”

title: “Monks, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because he…
content: “Monks, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because he sees this body composed of the four great elements increasing and decreasing, being taken up and discarded. Therefore, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding it. But regarding that which is called mind, intellect, consciousness — here, an untaught ordinary person is not capable of disenchantment, not capable of dispassion, not capable of liberation. Why is that? For a long time, monks, an untaught ordinary person has been attached, regarded as ‘mine,’ grasped at: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ Therefore, he is not capable of disenchantment, dispassion, or liberation regarding it.”

title: “And when, monks, the mind is freed from these five defilements — sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt — then it…
content: “And when, monks, the mind is freed from these five defilements — sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt — then it becomes malleable, wieldy, radiant, not brittle, properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. Regarding whatever state is to be directly known, the mind inclines to direct knowledge, and in each case he attains the ability and capacity to realize that state.”

title: “Vāseṭṭha, there are five factors that cause the growth of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye — desirable, beautiful, delightful, enticing, connected…
content: “Vāseṭṭha, there are five factors that cause the growth of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye — desirable, beautiful, delightful, enticing, connected with sensual pleasure and enjoyment; sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … touches cognizable by the body — desirable, beautiful, delightful, enticing, connected with sensual pleasure and enjoyment. Vāseṭṭha, those five factors that cause the growth of sensual pleasure — the brahmins proficient in the three Vedas, attached, infatuated, bound, not seeing their danger, not understanding the escape from them, enjoy them. Vāseṭṭha, that those brahmins proficient in the three Vedas, abandoning the qualities that make a brahmin, following qualities that do not make a brahmin, attached, infatuated, bound, not seeing their danger, not understanding the escape from them, enjoying them, bound by the bondage of sensual pleasures, could after death be reborn in union with Brahmā — such a thing is not possible.”

title: "O great king, when the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes…
content: "O great king, when the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — that cause the monk restrains, guards the eye faculty, practices the restraint of the eye faculty."

title: “Monks, what is a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future? Monks, there are some ascetics…
content: “Monks, what is a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future? Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine, such a view: ‘There is no fault in sensual pleasures.’ They indulge in sensual pleasures. Having indulged, at the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a plane of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell. There they experience painful, sharp, severe feelings. They say: ‘Those venerable ascetics and brahmins who see the future danger in sensual pleasures, who speak of the abandoning of sensual pleasures, who describe the full understanding of sensual pleasures—but we, with these sensual pleasures as the cause, as the condition, experience these painful, sharp, severe feelings.’ Monks, this is called a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future.”

title: “Cut down the forest, not just a tree — From the forest, fear is born. Having cut down both forest and undergrowth, Be forest-free, O…
content:
“Cut down the forest, not just a tree —
From the forest, fear is born.
Having cut down both forest and undergrowth,
Be forest-free, O monks.”

“As long as even the smallest desire
Of a man for women is not cut off,
His mind is bound like a suckling calf to its mother.”

“Cut off your affection,
Like plucking an autumn lotus with the hand.
Develop the path to peace, Nibbāna,
Taught by the Well-gone One.”

title: “Venerable sirs, what is the effort of abandoning? Here, a monk does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent.…
content: “Venerable sirs, what is the effort of abandoning? Here, a monk does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. He does not consent to arisen ill-will thought … he does not consent to arisen harmful thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. This, venerable sirs, is called the effort of abandoning.”

title: “Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises…
content: “Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — because of that, delight arises. Migajāla, I say that with the arising of delight, suffering arises. Sounds … Odors … Tastes … Touches … Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind … If a monk delights in them, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — because of that, delight arises. Migajāla, I say that with the arising of delight, suffering arises.”

title: “Here, monks, the second kind of ascetics and brahmins think: ‘These first ascetics and brahmins, entering and indulging, ate the bait … and have not…
content: “Here, monks, the second kind of ascetics and brahmins think: ‘These first ascetics and brahmins, entering and indulging, ate the bait … and have not escaped Māra’s power. Suppose we completely abandon the bait and the world’s offerings, abandon what is fearful, go into the forest and dwell.’ They completely abandon the bait and the world’s offerings, abandon what is fearful, go into the forest and dwell. There they become grass-eaters, millet-eaters, raw-rice eaters, Nivara-seed eaters, crust-eaters, husk-eaters, rice-scum eaters, sesame-seed eaters, grass-eaters, cow-dung eaters, forest roots and fruits eaters, fallen-fruit eaters. At the end of the summer, when water and grass become scarce, their bodies become extremely emaciated. Because their bodies become extremely emaciated, their energy for striving is exhausted. Because their energy is exhausted, their mind’s liberation is exhausted. Because their mind’s liberation is exhausted, they return to the bait cast by Māra and the world’s offerings. There they again enter, indulge, and eat those foods. By entering, indulging, and eating, they become infatuated; from infatuation, heedless; from heedlessness, subject to Māra’s will. Thus, monks, these second ascetics and brahmins have not escaped Māra’s power.”
